claim: Elevated pUb levels have been observed in aged human brains and in Parkinson's disease.
source: Elevated pUb levels have been observed in aged human brains and in Parkinson's disease, but the mechanistic link between pUb elevation and neurodegeneration remains unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Fiesel et al., 2015; Hou et al., 2018; Shiba-Fukushima et al., 2017) as stated in the Introduction section.

claim: Impaired proteasomal activity leads to the accumulation of sPINK1, the cytosolic form of PINK1 that is normally proteasome-degraded rapidly.
source: We show that impaired proteasomal activity leads to the accumulation of sPINK1, the cytosolic form of PINK1 that is normally proteasome-degraded rapidly.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including Western blot analyses showing sPINK1 accumulation upon MG132 treatment (Figure 2).

claim: sPINK1 accumulation increases ubiquitin phosphorylation, which then inhibits ubiquitin-dependent proteasomal activity by interfering with both ubiquitin chain elongation and proteasome-substrate interactions.
source: This accumulation increases ubiquitin phosphorylation, which then inhibits ubiquitin-dependent proteasomal activity by interfering with both ubiquitin chain elongation and proteasome-substrate interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental data including in vitro ubiquitin chain formation assays (Figure 3A), proteasomal degradation assays (Figure 3C), and TIRF microscopy (Figure 3D-I).

claim: Specific expression of sPINK1 in mouse hippocampal neurons induced progressive pUb accumulation, accompanied by protein aggregation, proteostasis disruption, neuronal injury, neuroinflammation, and cognitive decline.
source: Specific expression of sPINK1 in mouse hippocampal neurons induced progressive pUb accumulation, accompanied by protein aggregation, proteostasis disruption, neuronal injury, neuroinflammation, and cognitive decline.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from AAV-mediated sPINK1 expression in mouse hippocampus, including Western blots (Figure 6), immunofluorescence (Figures 5-8), behavioral tests (Figure 7A-D), and proteomic analysis (Figure 5).

claim: Pink1 knockout mitigated protein aggregation in both mouse brains and HEK293 cells.
source: Conversely, Pink1 knockout mitigated protein aggregation in both mouse brains and HEK293 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot and immunofluorescence data comparing wild-type and Pink1-/- mice and cells (Figure 4).

claim: The detrimental effects of sPINK1 could be counteracted by co-expressing Ub/S65A phospho-null mutant but exacerbated by over-expressing Ub/S65E phospho-mimic mutant.
source: Furthermore, the detrimental effects of sPINK1 could be counteracted by co-expressing Ub/S65A phospho-null mutant but exacerbated by over-expressing Ub/S65E phospho-mimic mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from AAV experiments with different ubiquitin mutants, including behavioral tests (Figure 7A-D), Western blots (Figure 6), and immunofluorescence (Figures 5-8).

claim: pUb elevation, triggered by reduced proteasomal activity, inhibits proteasomal activity and forms a feedforward loop that drives progressive neurodegeneration.
source: Together, these findings reveal that pUb elevation, triggered by reduced proteasomal activity, inhibits proteasomal activity and forms a feedforward loop that drives progressive neurodegeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by the integration of multiple experimental findings throughout the manuscript, including proteasomal activity assays, protein aggregation data, and in vivo neurodegeneration models.

claim: A marked elevation of both PINK1 and pUb was found in brain samples from AD patients in the cingulate gyrus brain regions with Aβ plaques, when compared to age- and sex-matched controls.
source: We found a marked elevation of both PINK1 and pUb in brain samples from AD patients in the cingulate gyrus brain regions with Aβ plaques, when compared to age- and sex-matched controls (Figure 1A and B; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from human brain samples shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Increased PINK1 and pUb levels could be detected in neocortex of APP/PS1 mouse brains with Aβ compared to wild-type mice.
source: This finding was corroborated in the APP/PS1 mouse model of AD, where increased PINK1 and pUb levels could be detected in neocortex of mouse brains with Aβ compared to wild-type mice (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from APP/PS1 mouse brains shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: PINK1 and pUb levels in neocortex of wild-type and Pink1-knockout mice differ little under physiological conditions.
source: On the other hand, PINK1 and pUb levels in neocortex of wild-type and Pink1-knockout mice (Pink1-/-) differ little (Figure 1C and D), which can be attributed to the low expression of PINK1 in normal mouse brains under physiological conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C and D, with an inference about low PINK1 expression under physiological conditions.

claim: A significant increase in neuronal pUb levels was observed in aged wild-type mouse compared to young mouse in neocortex of the brains.
source: However, we observed a significant increase in neuronal pUb levels in aged wild-type mouse compared to young mouse in neocortex of the brains (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and Western blot data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: pUb levels in Pink1-/- mice remained unchanged with age and were notably lower than those in aged wild-type mice.
source: As a control, pUb levels in Pink1-/- mice remained unchanged with age and were notably lower than those in aged wild-type mice (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and Western blot data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: A marked increase in both PINK1 and pUb levels was observed in the ischemic core of mouse brains compared to the contralateral cortex using mouse MCAO model.
source: Using mouse middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) model, we observed a marked increase in both PINK1 and pUb levels in the ischemic core of mouse brains compared to the contralateral cortex (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: OGD followed by reperfusion caused a time-dependent increase in PINK1, sPINK1, and pUb levels in HEK293 cells.
source: OGD followed by reperfusion caused a time-dependent increase in PINK1, sPINK1, and pUb levels (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: An increase in protein aggregation was observed following OGD and reperfusion, as evidenced by the accumulation of ubiquitin in the insoluble protein fraction.
source: Additionally, we observed an increase in protein aggregation, as evidenced by the accumulation of ubiquitin in the insoluble protein fraction (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Elevated pUb levels are a common feature across a wide spectrum of neurodegenerative conditions, both chronic and acute.
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that elevated pUb levels are a common feature across a wide spectrum of neurodegenerative conditions, both chronic and acute.
evidence: This claim is supported by the collective data from AD patients, aged mice, APP/PS1 mice, and MCAO models presented in Figure 1.

claim: Elevated pUb levels can result from either an elevated level of full-length PINK1 or sPINK1.
source: Elevated pUb levels can result from either an elevated level of full-length PINK1 or sPINK1.
evidence: This claim is based on the understanding of PINK1 biology and is supported by experimental data showing different conditions that increase PINK1 or sPINK1 (Figure 2A).

claim: PINK1 increase can occur upon mitochondrial injuries with the treatment of CCCP and O/A.
source: PINK1 increase can occur upon mitochondrial injuries with the treatment of CCCP and O/A, and sPINK1 increase can occur upon proteasomal inhibition with the treatment of MG132 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: sPINK1 increase can occur upon proteasomal inhibition with the treatment of MG132.
source: PINK1 increase can occur upon mitochondrial injuries with the treatment of CCCP and O/A, and sPINK1 increase can occur upon proteasomal inhibition with the treatment of MG132 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The treatment of MG132 caused a concentration- and time-dependent increase in sPINK1 and pUb levels in wild-type HEK293 cells, with sPINK1 levels plateaued at 6 hr.
source: The treatment of MG132 caused a concentration- and time-dependent increase in sPINK1 and pUb levels in wild-type HEK293 cells, with sPINK1 levels plateaued at 6 hr (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2B-E.

claim: PINK1 and pUb levels remained low in PINK1-knockout HEK293 cells upon the treatment of MG132.
source: In contrast, PINK1 and pUb levels remained low in PINK1-knockout HEK293 cells upon the treatment of MG132 (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2B-E.

claim: Elevated pUb levels were observed upon the transfection of full-length PINK1 and sPINK1*, with the latter more pronounced.
source: The analysis also showed elevated pUb levels upon the transfection of full-length PINK1 and sPINK1*, with the latter more pronounced.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Transfection with sPINK1*-KD or UbGG-sPINK1 had little effect on pUb levels.
source: In contrast, transfection with sPINK1*-KD or UbGG-sPINK1 had little effect on pUb levels (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Ubiquitin-positive puncta were observed following MG132 treatment or upon the transfection of sPINK1*.
source: In contrast, ubiquitin-positive puncta were observed following MG132 treatment or upon the transfection of sPINK1* (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: MG132 treatment and sPINK1* transfection, but not sPINK1*-KD or UbGG-sPINK1 transfection, increased ubiquitin levels in the insoluble protein fraction.
source: Furthermore, Western blot analysis showed that MG132 treatment and sPINK1* transfection (Figure 2H), but not sPINK1*-KD or UbGG-sPINK1 transfection, increased ubiquitin levels in the insoluble protein fraction.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: There is a positive correlation between PINK1 and pUb levels and the aggregation of ubiquitinated proteins.
source: These findings suggest a positive correlation between PINK1 and pUb levels and the aggregation of ubiquitinated proteins, which likely results from an impairment of proteasomal activity, akin to the effect of MG132.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that conditions increasing PINK1/pUb also increase protein aggregation (Figure 2).

claim: Transfection with sPINK1* caused GFP accumulation in cells transfected with Ub-R-GFP.
source: Transfection with sPINK1* also caused GFP accumulation, but the transfection of sPINK1*-KD did not (Figure 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: sPINK1* transfection leads to increased pUb levels and impairs proteasomal degradation.
source: Thus, sPINK1* transfection leads to increased pUb levels and impairs proteasomal degradation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the Ub-R-GFP degradation assay data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: While sPINK1* can enhance autophagic degradation of ubiquitinated proteins, potentially through p62 phosphorylation, elevated PINK1 and pUb levels cause an inhibition of proteasomal degradation.
source: Taken together, the findings demonstrate that while sPINK1* can enhance autophagic degradation of ubiquitinated proteins, potentially through p62 phosphorylation as previously reported (Gao et al., 2016), elevated PINK1 and pUb levels cause an inhibition of proteasomal degradation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the puromycin/BALA experiment data shown in Figure 2J and cited literature (Gao et al., 2016).

claim: pUb predominantly formed di-Ub chains while unmodified ubiquitin efficiently formed di-, tri-, and higher-order chains catalyzed by E1 and E2 enzymes.
source: While the unmodified ubiquitin efficiently formed di-, tri-, and higher-order chains catalyzed by E1 and E2 enzymes, pUb predominantly formed di-Ub chains (Figure 3A), consistent with the previous report (Wauer et al., 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by Coomassie blue staining data shown in Figure 3A and cited literature (Wauer et al., 2015b).

claim: Ub/S65A mutation did not affect chain elongation, producing a polyUb ladder similar to unmodified ubiquitin, while Ub/S65E mutation only formed di-Ub.
source: The introduction of S65A (phospho-null) and S65E (phospho-mimetic) ubiquitin mutants further confirmed the impact of phosphorylation—Ub/S65A mutation did not affect chain elongation, producing a polyUb ladder similar to unmodified ubiquitin, while Ub/S65E mutation only formed di-Ub (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Coomassie blue staining data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: K48-linked chains were observed in wild-type and PINK1-/- cells upon proteasomal inhibition with MG132, but were absent in cells over-expressing full-length PINK1 or sPINK1*.
source: Upon proteasomal inhibition with MG132, K48-linked chains were observed in wild-type and PINK1-/- cells, but were absent in cells over-expressing full-length PINK1 or sPINK1* (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The degradation of K48-linked pUb-chain-modified GFP (pK48-polyUb-GFP) was slower compared to its unmodified counterpart (K48-polyUb-GFP) in an in vitro degradation assay using purified proteasomes.
source: Using an in vitro degradation assay using purified proteasomes, we found that the degradation of K48-linked pUb-chain-modified GFP (pK48-polyUb-GFP) was slower compared to its unmodified counterpart (K48-polyUb-GFP) (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3C and supplementary figures.

claim: TIRF microscopy assay revealed fewer GFP puncta for pK48-polyUb-GFP compared to K48-polyUb-GFP.
source: The assay revealed fewer GFP puncta for pK48-polyUb-GFP compared to K48-polyUb-GFP (Figure 3D, E, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 3D, E, and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The GFP puncta for pK48-polyUb-GFP dissociated more rapidly from the proteasomes, reflecting a shorter dwell time of the proteasome-substrate complex.
source: Furthermore, the GFP puncta for pK48-polyUb-GFP dissociated more rapidly from the proteasomes, reflecting a shorter dwell time of the proteasome-substrate complex (Figure 3F–I, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by TIRF microscopy time-trace data shown in Figure 3F-I and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Phosphorylation impairs the noncovalent interactions between polyUb chains conjugated to substrate proteins and the ubiquitin receptors residing in the proteasome.
source: Thus, phosphorylation impairs the noncovalent interactions between polyUb chains conjugated to substrate proteins and the ubiquitin receptors residing in the proteasome.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the TIRF microscopy data showing reduced binding and shorter dwell times for pK48-polyUb-GFP (Figure 3D-I).

claim: Elevated pUb levels disrupt proteasomal function through two distinct mechanisms: impairing covalent ubiquitin chain elongation and substrate ubiquitination, as well as weakening non-covalent interactions between ubiquitinated substrates and the proteasome.
source: Together, these findings demonstrate that elevated pUb levels disrupt proteasomal function through two distinct mechanisms: impairing covalent ubiquitin chain elongation and substrate ubiquitination, as well as weakening non-covalent interactions between ubiquitinated substrates and the proteasome.
evidence: This claim is supported by the collective data from ubiquitin chain formation assays (Figure 3A, B) and proteasome-substrate interaction assays (Figure 3C-I).

claim: Insoluble ubiquitin levels accumulated significantly slower in PINK1-/- cells compared to wild-type cells upon MG132 treatment, though eventually reaching levels comparable to those in wild-type cells.
source: However, insoluble ubiquitin levels accumulated significantly slower in PINK1-/- cells, though eventually reaching levels comparable to those in wild-type cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: PINK1 deficiency delays the accumulation of protein aggregates.
source: This not only confirms that PINK1/pUb operates within the same pathway as MG132—the proteasome—but also demonstrates that PINK1 deficiency delays the accumulation of protein aggregates.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the Western blot data showing delayed accumulation of insoluble ubiquitin in PINK1-/- cells (Figure 4A, B).

claim: LC3-II levels did not increase in PINK1-/- cells following MG132 treatment.
source: However, LC3-II levels did not increase in PINK1-/- cells following MG132 treatment (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: PINK1 plays a critical role in the activation of autophagy.
source: This confirms the critical role of PINK1 in the activation of autophagy (Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the LC3-II data (Figure 4C, D) and supported by the puromycin/BALA experiment (Figure 2J).

claim: Aged Pink1-/- mice showed no age-related changes in neuronal ubiquitin distribution or insoluble ubiquitin levels.
source: In contrast, aged Pink1-/- mice showed no such age-related changes in neuronal ubiquitin distribution or insoluble ubiquitin levels (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and Western blot data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Following MCAO, insoluble ubiquitin levels were significantly elevated in the ipsilateral hemisphere of wild-type mice compared to sham and contralateral hemisphere, but remained unchanged in Pink1-/- mice.
source: Following MCAO, insoluble ubiquitin levels were significantly elevated in the ipsilateral hemisphere of wild-type mice compared to sham and contralateral hemisphere, but remained unchanged in Pink1-/- mice (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Pink1 knockout disrupts the cycle of proteasomal inhibition and pUb accumulation, thereby alleviating proteasomal inhibition and mitigating protein aggregation under neurodegenerative conditions.
source: Together, our results reveal that Pink1 knockout disrupts this cycle, thereby alleviating proteasomal inhibition and mitigating protein aggregation under these conditions, further demonstrating the critical role of pUb in this process.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective data showing reduced protein aggregation in Pink1-/- mice and cells under various neurodegenerative conditions (Figure 4).

claim: Overexpression of sPINK1* or Ub/S65E induced the formation of ubiquitin-positive puncta in SH-SY5Y cells, similar to the effects of MG132 treatment.
source: Overexpression of sPINK1* or Ub/S65E induced the formation of ubiquitin-positive puncta in cells, similar to the effects of MG132 treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and the observations in HEK293 cells (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Over-expression of Ub/S65E caused significant neuronal loss at 30 and 70 days post-transfection, but not in the other three groups (control, sPINK1*, sPINK1*+Ub/S65A).
source: While no visible changes were observed at 10 days post-transfection, significant neuronal loss, based on NeuN immunofluorescence staining, was evident at 30 and 70 days in mice expressing Ub/S65E, but not in other three groups (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ub/S65E induced glial responses at 30- and 70 days post-transfection, based on GFAP/Iba1 immunofluorescence staining and GFAP/CD11b Western blot bands.
source: Additionally, Ub/S65E induced glial responses at 30- and 70 days post-transfection, based on GFAP/Iba1 immunofluorescence staining and GFAP/CD11b Western blot bands (Figure 5—figure supplements 3 and 4, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: The sPINK1* and sPINK1*+Ub/S65A groups showed an increase in GFAP levels at 70 days post-transfection with no changes in Iba1 or CD11b levels, suggesting potential neuronal injury.
source: In contrast, the sPINK1* and sPINK1*+Ub/S65A groups showed an increase in GFAP levels at 70 days post-transfection with no changes in Iba1 or CD11b levels, suggesting potential neuronal injury (Figure 5—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 3 and 4, with an inference about neuronal injury.

claim: The neuronal injury and neuroinflammation marker HMGB1 was elevated at both 30 and 70 days following sPINK1* overexpression.
source: For example, the neuronal injury and neuroinflammation marker HMGB1 was elevated at both time points following sPINK1* overexpression, while the mitochondrial marker Tom20 showed a delayed decrease at 70 days, indicative of mitochondrial loss.
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: The mitochondrial marker Tom20 showed a delayed decrease at 70 days following sPINK1* overexpression, indicative of mitochondrial loss.
source: For example, the neuronal injury and neuroinflammation marker HMGB1 was elevated at both time points following sPINK1* overexpression, while the mitochondrial marker Tom20 showed a delayed decrease at 70 days, indicative of mitochondrial loss.
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: At 30 days post-transfection of sPINK1*, changes in proteins associated with mitophagy, mitochondrial organization, and respiratory electron transport were observed, suggesting an initial injury and compensatory response to mitochondrial stress.
source: At 30 days, changes in proteins associated with mitophagy, mitochondrial organization, and respiratory electron transport were observed, suggesting an initial injury and compensatory response to mitochondrial stress (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis data shown in Figure 5E, with an inference about initial injury and compensatory response.

claim: By 70 days post-transfection of sPINK1*, changes in mitochondrial proteins expanded to include broader mitochondrial dysfunction and apoptotic processes, ultimately leading to mitochondrial loss and neuronal injury.
source: By 70 days, these changes expanded to include broader mitochondrial dysfunction and apoptotic processes, ultimately leading to mitochondrial loss and neuronal injury (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis data shown in Figure 5E, with an inference about the progression to mitochondrial loss and neuronal injury.

claim: At 70 days post-transfection of sPINK1*, a large number of proteins were either upregulated or downregulated, indicative of disrupted proteostasis.
source: At 70 days post-transfection, a large number of proteins were either upregulated or downregulated, indicative of disrupted proteostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis data shown in Figure 5F-H.

claim: A significant up-regulation of RNA-binding and RNA-processing proteins was observed at 70 days post-transfection of sPINK1*.
source: For example, we observed a significant up-regulation of RNA-binding and RNA-processing proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis data shown in Figure 5F-H.

claim: Many of the up-regulated proteins at 70 days post-transfection of sPINK1* were associated with impaired synaptic functions and neuronal projections.
source: Significantly, many of the up-regulated proteins were associated with impaired synaptic functions and neuronal projections, while down-regulated proteins were linked to myelination, synaptic maturation, and lipid metabolism (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis data shown in Figure 5F-H.

claim: Down-regulated proteins at 70 days post-transfection of sPINK1* were linked to myelination, synaptic maturation, and lipid metabolism.
source: Significantly, many of the up-regulated proteins were associated with impaired synaptic functions and neuronal projections, while down-regulated proteins were linked to myelination, synaptic maturation, and lipid metabolism (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis data shown in Figure 5F-H.

claim: The proteomics data indicate a systemic and time-dependent impact upon sPINK1* over-expression on neuronal structure and function, leading to cumulative neuronal injury that mirrors the progressive pathogenesis of neurodegeneration.
source: As these changes were insignificant at 30 days post-transfection (Figure 5F–H), the proteomics data indicate a systemic and time-dependent impact upon sPINK1* over-expression on neuronal structure and function, leading to cumulative neuronal injury that mirrors the progressive pathogenesis of neurodegeneration.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of proteomic changes at 30 and 70 days post-transfection (Figure 5F-H).

claim: At 30 days following sPINK1* transfection, a distinct band for sPINK1 was observed, accompanied by a significant increase in pUb levels.
source: At 30 days following sPINK1* transfection, a distinct band for sPINK1 was observed, accompanied by a significant increase in pUb levels (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: At 70 days following sPINK1* transfection, three distinct bands could be observed that likely correspond to sPINK1, full-length PINK1, and ubiquitinated PINK1.
source: At 70 days following sPINK1* transfection, three distinct bands could be observed that likely correspond to sPINK1, full-length PINK1, and ubiquitinated PINK1 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6B, with an inference about the identity of the bands.

claim: The presence of full-length PINK1 at 70 days following sPINK1* transfection indicates mitochondrial injury.
source: The presence of full-length PINK1 indicates mitochondrial injury, and ubiquitinated PINK1 indicates compromised proteasomal activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the Western blot data (Figure 6B) and established knowledge about PINK1 biology.

claim: Ubiquitinated PINK1 at 70 days following sPINK1* transfection indicates compromised proteasomal activity.
source: The presence of full-length PINK1 indicates mitochondrial injury, and ubiquitinated PINK1 indicates compromised proteasomal activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the Western blot data (Figure 6B) and established knowledge about proteasomal degradation.

claim: The pUb levels were increased by 43.8% and 59.9% compared to the control at 30- and 70-days following sPINK1* transfection, respectively.
source: The pUb levels were increased by 43.8% and 59.9% compared to the control at 30- and 70-days following sPINK1* transfection, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A and C.

claim: The pUb level remained at the control level with the Ub/S65A mutant co-expressed with sPINK1*.
source: In comparison, the pUb level remained at the control level with the Ub/S65A mutant co-expressed with sPINK1* (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Ub/S65A counteracts the proteasomal inhibition induced by sPINK1*, thereby promoting the degradation of sPINK1* and prevent pUb accumulation.
source: Thus, Ub/S65A counteracts the proteasomal inhibition induced by sPINK1*, thereby promoting the degradation of sPINK1* and prevent pUb accumulation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the Western blot data showing reduced sPINK1 and pUb levels with Ub/S65A co-expression (Figure 6B, C).

claim: The levels of ubiquitin in the insoluble protein fraction were significantly elevated in the sPINK1*, sPINK1*+Ub/S65A, and Ub/S65E groups.
source: On the other hand, the levels of ubiquitin in the insoluble protein fraction were significantly elevated in the sPINK1*, sPINK1*+Ub/S65A, and Ub/S65E groups (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Proteins smaller than 70 kDa accumulated in the sPINK1* and Ub/S65E groups, indicating an inhibition of ubiquitin chain elongation, but not in the sPINK1*+Ub/S65A group.
source: Notably, proteins smaller than 70 kDa accumulated in the sPINK1* and Ub/S65E groups, indicating an inhibition of ubiquitin chain elongation, consistent with our findings obtained in vitro (Figure 3B), but not in the sPINK1*+Ub/S65A group.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6F and comparison with in vitro data (Figure 3B).

claim: Overexpression of Ub/S65E resulted in significant neuronal death and glial proliferation.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of Ub/S65E resulted in significant neuronal death and glial proliferation (Figure 6D, Figure 5—figure supplements 2–4), despite that the overall pUb levels appear unchanged at 70 days post-transfection (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 5—figure supplements 2-4.

claim: Overexpression of sPINK1*, sPINK1*+Ub/S65A, or Ub/S65E had minimal effects on autophagic flux at the animal level, as evidenced by unchanged LC3-II and p62 levels in both soluble and insoluble protein fractions.
source: It should be noted that overexpression of sPINK1*, sPINK1*+Ub/S65A, or Ub/S65E had minimal effects on autophagic flux at the animal level, as evidenced by unchanged LC3-II and p62 levels in both soluble and insoluble protein fractions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Protein aggregation driven by elevated pUb levels primarily results from the inhibition of proteasomal degradation in the brains of animal or human with neurodegenerative conditions.
source: This contrasts with the findings in cultured cells (Figure 4C and D), and suggests that, mechanistically, protein aggregation driven by elevated pUb levels primarily results from the inhibition of proteasomal degradation in the brains of animal or human with neurodegenerative conditions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of autophagy markers in cells versus animals (Figure 4C, D vs. Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: Over-expression of sPINK1* or Ub/S65E significantly reduced the number of sniffs toward the novel object in novel object recognition test compared to the control mice or the old object.
source: Over-expression of sPINK1* or Ub/S65E significantly reduced the number of sniffs toward the novel object in novel object recognition test compared to the control mice or the old object (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: Over-expression of sPINK1* or Ub/S65E significantly reduced freezing time in the fear conditioning test compared to control mice.
source: In the fear conditioning test, over-expression of sPINK1* or Ub/S65E also significantly reduced freezing time compared to control mice (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: Both sPINK1* and Ub/S65E overexpression impaired cognitive functions of mice.
source: These findings indicate that both sPINK1* and Ub/S65E overexpression impaired cognitive functions of mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the behavioral test data showing impaired performance in novel object recognition and fear conditioning tests (Figure 7A-D).

claim: Co-expression of Ub/S65A with sPINK1* ameliorated sPINK1*-induced cognitive deficits, suggesting a protective effect against pUb-caused impairments.
source: Moreover, co-expression of Ub/S65A with sPINK1* ameliorated sPINK1*-induced cognitive deficits, suggesting a protective effect against pUb-caused impairments (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 7A-D.

claim: Western blot analysis showed decreased levels of Tom20, a mitochondrial marker, in brains over-expressing sPINK1*.
source: Consistent with the proteomics analysis (Figure 5), Western blot analysis showed decreased levels of Tom20, a mitochondrial marker, in brains over-expressing sPINK1* (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7E and is consistent with proteomic data (Figure 5).

claim: The mitochondrial deficit induced by sPINK1* overexpression could be reversed by co-expressing Ub/S65A.
source: Notably, the mitochondrial deficit induced by sPINK1* overexpression could be reversed by co-expressing Ub/S65A (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Reduced levels of MAP2, a dendritic marker, and PSD95, a postsynaptic density marker, were observed in the hippocampus of mice over-expressing sPINK1* and Ub/S65E.
source: Furthermore, we observed reduced levels of MAP2, a dendritic marker, and PSD95, a postsynaptic density marker, in the hippocampus of mice over-expressing sPINK1* and Ub/S65E.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7F and G.

claim: The reductions in MAP2 and PSD95 could be restored by co-expressing Ub/S65A with sPINK1*.
source: The reductions could be restored by co-expressing Ub/S65A with sPINK1* (Figure 7F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7F and G.

claim: sPINK1* overexpression induced neuronal injury originating from the nerve terminals, recapitulating neurodegenerative changes.
source: Together, these findings indicate that sPINK1* overexpression induced neuronal injury originating from the nerve terminals, recapitulating neurodegenerative changes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective data showing reduced synaptic and dendritic markers (Figure 7E-G) and spine loss (Figure 7H).

claim: Golgi staining revealed a reduction in dendritic spine density following sPINK1* overexpression, which was reversed by co-expressing Ub/S65A.
source: The staining revealed a reduction in dendritic spine density following sPINK1* overexpression, which was reversed by co-expressing Ub/S65A (Figure 7H).
evidence: This claim is supported by Golgi staining data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Ub/S65E over-expression resulted in severe dendritic and spine loss, characterized by marked slimmer dendrites and a significant reduction in spine density.
source: In contrast, Ub/S65E over-expression resulted in severe dendritic and spine loss, characterized by marked slimmer dendrites and a significant reduction in spine density (Figure 7H).
evidence: This claim is supported by Golgi staining data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Proteomic analysis revealed a >54-fold increase in CamK2n1 (Calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II inhibitor 1) upon sPINK1* over-expression.
source: Notably, our proteomics analysis revealed a >54-fold increase in CamK2n1 (Calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II inhibitor 1, Uniprot Q6QWF9) upon sPINK1* over-expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data from the manuscript.

claim: CamK2n1 is an endogenous inhibitor of CamKII.
source: CamK2n1 is an endogenous inhibitor of CamKII (Gouet et al., 2012), and CamKII is essential for synapse formation, neuronal plasticity, and long-term potentiation (Hell, 2014; O'Day, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Gouet et al., 2012).

claim: CamKII is essential for synapse formation, neuronal plasticity, and long-term potentiation.
source: CamK2n1 is an endogenous inhibitor of CamKII (Gouet et al., 2012), and CamKII is essential for synapse formation, neuronal plasticity, and long-term potentiation (Hell, 2014; O'Day, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Hell, 2014; O'Day, 2022).

claim: The activation of CamKII requires the targeted degradation of CamK2n1 by the proteasome.
source: As illustrated in Figure 8A, the activation of CamKII requires the targeted degradation of CamK2n1 by the proteasome (Buard et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Buard et al., 2010) and illustrated in Figure 8A.

claim: The increase of phosphorylated CamKII initiates the CREB signal pathway, representing a key mechanism in synaptic plasticity.
source: Then, the increase of phosphorylated CamKII subsequently initiates the CREB signal pathway, representing a key mechanism in synaptic plasticity (Davidson and Pickering, 2023; Ortega-Martínez, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Davidson and Pickering, 2023; Ortega-Martínez, 2015).

claim: The overexpression of sPINK1* increases pUb level, which can inhibit CamK2n1 degradation and suppress the activation of CamKII-CREB signal pathway.
source: The overexpression of sPINK1* increases pUb level, which can inhibit CamK2n1 degradation and suppress the activation of CamKII-CREB signal pathway.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the mechanism illustrated in Figure 8A and supported by experimental data showing elevated CamK2n1 and reduced pCamKII and pCREB (Figure 8B-E).

claim: Immunofluorescence staining confirmed the elevated CamK2n1 levels in hippocampus CA1 neurons at 70 days post-transfection of sPINK1* compared to the controls.
source: Immunofluorescence staining confirmed the elevated CamK2n1 levels in hippocampus CA1 neurons at 70 days post-transfection of sPINK1* compared to the controls (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The increase in CamK2n1 was accompanied by reduced levels of phosphorylated CamKII (pCamKII) and phosphorylated CREB (pCREB).
source: This increase was accompanied by reduced levels of phosphorylated CamKII (pCamKII) (Figure 8C) and phosphorylated CREB (pCREB) (Figure 8D), the latter of which was confirmed by Western blotting (Figure 8E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and Western blot data shown in Figure 8C-E.

claim: sPINK1* over-expression led to reduced levels of BDNF and ERK, all downstream targets of CREB signaling.
source: Furthermore, sPINK1* over-expression led to reduced levels of BDNF and ERK, all downstream targets of CREB signaling (Figure 8F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8F and G.

claim: Impaired degradation of CamK2n1 disrupts CamKII-CREB signaling, contributing to the structural deficits in dendritic spines, postsynaptic density, and neuronal projection.
source: These findings suggest that impaired degradation of CamK2n1 disrupts CamKII-CREB signaling, contributing to the structural deficits in dendritic spines, postsynaptic density, and neuronal projection.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective data showing elevated CamK2n1, reduced pCamKII/pCREB/BDNF/ERK, and structural deficits (Figure 8).

claim: Mitochondrial injury has been established as a mechanism that causes pUb elevation.
source: While mitochondrial injury has been established as a mechanism that causes pUb elevation (Chin et al., 2023; Lambourne et al., 2023), we have identified an additional pathway—the inhibition of proteasomal degradation leads to the stabilization of sPINK1 in the cytoplasm, where it remains active and phosphorylates ubiquitin.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Chin et al., 2023; Lambourne et al., 2023).

claim: The inhibition of proteasomal degradation leads to the stabilization of sPINK1 in the cytoplasm, where it remains active and phosphorylates ubiquitin.
source: While mitochondrial injury has been established as a mechanism that causes pUb elevation (Chin et al., 2023; Lambourne et al., 2023), we have identified an additional pathway—the inhibition of proteasomal degradation leads to the stabilization of sPINK1 in the cytoplasm, where it remains active and phosphorylates ubiquitin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing sPINK1 accumulation and pUb elevation upon proteasomal inhibition (Figure 2).

claim: Proteasomal inhibition can arise from many different pathological factors associated with neurodegeneration.
source: Proteasomal inhibition can arise from many different pathological factors associated with neurodegeneration (Cookson et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Cookson et al., 2023).

claim: Cerebral ischemia can cause ATP deficiency, and hypoxia and other secondary effect from oxidative stress can further modify the proteasome and impair its function.
source: For example, cerebral ischemia can cause ATP deficiency, and hypoxia and other secondary effect from oxidative stress can further modify the proteasome and impair its function (Chen et al., 2020; Wojcik and Di Napoli, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Chen et al., 2020; Wojcik and Di Napoli, 2004).

claim: In AD, amyloid fibrils can impair proteasomal activities by obstructing the proteasome's substrate entry channel.
source: In AD, amyloid fibrils can impair proteasomal activities by obstructing the proteasome's substrate entry channel (McDade et al., 2024; Tseng et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (McDade et al., 2024; Tseng et al., 2008).

claim: Elevated pUb levels have been proposed as a biomarker of neurodegeneration.
source: Indeed, the elevated pUb levels have been proposed as a biomarker of neurodegeneration (Fiesel et al., 2015; Hou et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Fiesel et al., 2015; Hou et al., 2018).

claim: Elevated pUb levels may actively contribute to the progression of neurodegenerative diseases.
source: As such, elevated pUb levels may actively contribute to the progression of neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence: This claim is speculative based on the understanding of ubiquitin function and is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Elevated pUb levels inhibit proteasomal activity, leading to protein aggregation and neuronal damages.
source: Furthermore, we reveal that elevated pUb levels inhibit proteasomal activity, leading to protein aggregation and neuronal damages.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental data including proteasomal activity assays, protein aggregation measurements, and neuronal injury markers throughout the manuscript.

claim: Ubiquitin phosphorylation disrupts the covalent elongation of ubiquitin chains.
source: Mechanistically, we show that ubiquitin phosphorylation disrupts two critical processes: (1) the covalent elongation of ubiquitin chains, as previously reported (Wauer et al., 2015b), and (2) the non-covalent interaction between K48-linked polyUb chains and the proteasome, a novel finding in this study.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro ubiquitin chain formation assays (Figure 3A, B) and cited literature (Wauer et al., 2015b).

claim: Ubiquitin phosphorylation disrupts the non-covalent interaction between K48-linked polyUb chains and the proteasome.
source: Mechanistically, we show that ubiquitin phosphorylation disrupts two critical processes: (1) the covalent elongation of ubiquitin chains, as previously reported (Wauer et al., 2015b), and (2) the non-covalent interaction between K48-linked polyUb chains and the proteasome, a novel finding in this study.
evidence: This claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data showing reduced binding and shorter dwell times (Figure 3D-I).

claim: This dual inhibitory mechanism interferes with the ubiquitination of substrate proteins, the recruitment of ubiquitinated proteins to the proteasome, and ultimately, the proteasomal degradation of substrate proteins.
source: This dual inhibitory mechanism interferes with the ubiquitination of substrate proteins, the recruitment of ubiquitinated proteins to the proteasome, and ultimately, the proteasomal degradation of substrate proteins.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective data on ubiquitin chain formation and proteasome-substrate interactions (Figure 3).

claim: Impaired proteasomal activity further impedes sPINK1 degradation, creating a self-amplifying cycle that drives pUb elevation and progressive proteasomal dysfunction.
source: Impaired proteasomal activity further impedes sPINK1 degradation, creating a self-amplifying cycle that drives pUb elevation and progressive proteasomal dysfunction.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective data showing that proteasomal inhibition leads to sPINK1 accumulation, which increases pUb, which further inhibits the proteasome.

claim: Cells have built-in stress responses to perturbation of the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
source: Although cells have built-in stress responses to perturbation of the ubiquitin-proteasome system (Hegde et al., 1993; Rai et al., 2025), the disruption caused by elevated pUb levels targets ubiquitin—the central player in the system—and is self-amplifying as proteasomal function deteriorates.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Hegde et al., 1993; Rai et al., 2025).

claim: The disruption caused by elevated pUb levels targets ubiquitin—the central player in the system—and is self-amplifying as proteasomal function deteriorates.
source: Although cells have built-in stress responses to perturbation of the ubiquitin-proteasome system (Hegde et al., 1993; Rai et al., 2025), the disruption caused by elevated pUb levels targets ubiquitin—the central player in the system—and is self-amplifying as proteasomal function deteriorates.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing the feedforward loop of pUb elevation and proteasomal inhibition.

claim: pUb plays a neuroprotective role, wherein PINK1 activation in response to mitochondrial damage results in the phosphorylation of ubiquitin and Parkin, initiating mitophagy to remove damaged mitochondria.
source: Extensive literature has reported that pUb plays a neuroprotective role, wherein PINK1 activation in response to mitochondrial damage results in the phosphorylation of ubiquitin and Parkin, initiating mitophagy to remove damaged mitochondria (Agarwal and Muqit, 2022; Li et al., 2023; Shiba-Fukushima et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Agarwal and Muqit, 2022; Li et al., 2023; Shiba-Fukushima et al., 2014).

claim: PINK1 deficiency has been linked to neurodegeneration, prompting the development of small-molecule activators.
source: Accordingly, PINK1 deficiency has been linked to neurodegeneration, prompting the development of small-molecule activators (Chin et al., 2023; Hertz et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Chin et al., 2023; Hertz et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023).

claim: Over-expression of sPINK1 resulted in chronic neuronal injury, driven by the reciprocal relationship between proteasomal inhibition and pUb elevation.
source: However, in the current study, over-expression of sPINK1 resulted in chronic neuronal injury, driven by the reciprocal relationship between proteasomal inhibition and pUb elevation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from AAV-mediated sPINK1 expression experiments showing progressive neuronal injury (Figures 5-8).

claim: The progressive decline of proteasomal activity disrupts cellular proteostasis, leading to the accumulation of protein aggregates.
source: The progressive decline of proteasomal activity disrupts cellular proteostasis, leading to the accumulation of protein aggregates.
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data (Figure 5) and protein aggregation measurements (Figure 6).

claim: Impaired proteasomal activity hinders the degradation of inhibitory proteins and consequently block the activation of key signaling pathways essential for neurogenesis and memory formation.
source: In addition to the mechanism of causing mitochondrial damage and inflammation by the protein aggregates, impaired proteasomal activity hinders the degradation of inhibitory proteins and consequently block the activation of key signaling pathways essential for neurogenesis and memory formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing elevated CamK2n1 and reduced CamKII-CREB signaling (Figure 8).

claim: PINK1 can function beyond the established role in mitophagy.
source: Collectively, our findings reveal that PINK1 can function beyond the established role in mitophagy, and elevated pUb levels are not simply a biomarker of neurodegeneration but a driving force behind progressive neuronal injury and neuroinflammation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing neurotoxic effects of sPINK1 overexpression independent of mitophagy.

claim: Elevated pUb levels are not simply a biomarker of neurodegeneration but a driving force behind progressive neuronal injury and neuroinflammation.
source: Collectively, our findings reveal that PINK1 can function beyond the established role in mitophagy, and elevated pUb levels are not simply a biomarker of neurodegeneration but a driving force behind progressive neuronal injury and neuroinflammation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the collective experimental data showing that elevated pUb causes proteasomal inhibition, protein aggregation, and neuronal injury.

claim: The neurotoxic effect upon sPINK1 over-expression is mediated through the ubiquitin phosphorylation.
source: The neurotoxic effect upon sPINK1 over-expression is mediated through the ubiquitin phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that Ub/S65A co-expression rescues the neurotoxic effects while Ub/S65E exacerbates them (Figures 6-7).

claim: Co-expression of the phospho-null mutant Ub/S65A restored proteasomal activity and even promoted the degradation of the rather stable sPINK1 variant used in the current study.
source: Co-expression of the phospho-null mutant Ub/S65A restored proteasomal activity and even promoted the degradation of the rather stable sPINK1 variant used in the current study.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data showing reduced sPINK1 levels with Ub/S65A co-expression (Figure 6B).

claim: Ub/S65A co-expression permitted the formation of longer polyUb chains, further supporting its role in antagonizing ubiquitin phosphorylation.
source: Additionally, Ub/S65A co-expression permitted the formation of longer polyUb chains, further supporting its role in antagonizing ubiquitin phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data showing different ubiquitin chain length distributions (Figure 6F).

claim: Over-expression of the phospho-mimetic Ub/S65E mutant caused more severe neuronal damage than sPINK1* overexpression.
source: In contrast, over-expression of the phospho-mimetic Ub/S65E mutant caused more severe neuronal damage than sPINK1* overexpression.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral tests, immunofluorescence, and Golgi staining data (Figures 5-7).

claim: The difference in neurotoxicity between Ub/S65E and sPINK1* can be attributed to the 100% increase in pUb mimicry with Ub/S65E, whereas sPINK1*-induced pUb levels are relatively low and subjected to dephosphorylation.
source: The difference can be attributed to the 100% increase in pUb mimicry with Ub/S65E, whereas sPINK1*-induced pUb levels are relatively low and subjected to dephosphorylation (Wall et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data and supported by citations about pUb dephosphorylation (Wall et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2018).

claim: sPINK1* can phosphorylate both free and substrate-conjugated Ub, whereas Ub/S65E only mimics monomeric pUb, further contributing to the heightened detrimental effects of the Ub/S65E mutant.
source: Moreover, sPINK1* can phosphorylate both free and substrate-conjugated Ub, whereas Ub/S65E only mimics monomeric pUb, further contributing to the heightened detrimental effects of the Ub/S65E mutant.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the understanding of PINK1 activity and the nature of the Ub/S65E mutant.

claim: Similar toxic effects of Ub/S65E over-expression has been reported in yeast.
source: Similar toxic effects of Ub/S65E over-expression has been reported in yeast (Swaney et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Swaney et al., 2015).

claim: A novel pathogenetic mechanism of neurodegeneration has been revealed, driven by a self-amplifying cycle of elevated pUb levels and proteasomal inhibition.
source: In conclusion, our findings have revealed a novel pathogenetic mechanism of neurodegeneration, driven by a self-amplifying cycle of elevated pUb levels and proteasomal inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by the collective experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: This cycle leads to the progressive decline of proteasomal activity and the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates, which may underlie both the sequelae of acute insults and the chronic progression of neurodegenerative diseases.
source: This cycle leads to the progressive decline of proteasomal activity and the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates, which may underlie both the sequelae of acute insults and the chronic progression of neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing progressive effects in both acute (MCAO) and chronic (aging, AD) models.

claim: pUb is not merely a consequence of neurodegeneration but also a critical driver of disease progression.
source: Our results demonstrate that pUb is not merely a consequence of this process but also a critical driver of disease progression.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing that pUb elevation causes proteasomal inhibition and neuronal injury.

claim: Targeting the pUb-mediated self-amplifying cycle represents a promising therapeutic strategy to slow or halt the progression of neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Therefore, targeting the pUb-mediated self-amplifying cycle represents a promising therapeutic strategy to slow or halt the progression of neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence: This claim is speculative based on the findings of the study.

claim: Neurodegeneration is characterized by irreversible loss of neurons, ultimately leading to cognitive and motor impairments.
source: Neurodegeneration, a hallmark of aging and neurodegenerative diseases, is characterized by irreversible loss of neurons, ultimately leading to cognitive and motor impairments (Cookson et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Cookson et al., 2023).

claim: A common feature of neurodegeneration is the accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins, often resulting from the impairment of protein degradation machineries, particularly the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS).
source: A common feature of neurodegeneration is the accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins, often resulting from the impairment of protein degradation machineries, particularly the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) (Davidson and Pickering, 2023; Kinger et al., 2024; McDade et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Davidson and Pickering, 2023; Kinger et al., 2024; McDade et al., 2024).

claim: The UPS is essential for maintaining cellular proteostasis, as it not only eliminates misfolded and toxic proteins but also dynamically regulates neuronal structure and function through controlled protein degradation.
source: The UPS is essential for maintaining cellular proteostasis, as it not only eliminates misfolded and toxic proteins but also dynamically regulates neuronal structure and function through controlled protein degradation (Costa et al., 2019; Krishna et al., 2022; Soykan et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Costa et al., 2019; Krishna et al., 2022; Soykan et al., 2021).

claim: Substrate proteins targeted for proteasomal degradation are typically conjugated with K48-linked polyubiquitin chains, which interact non-covalently with ubiquitin receptors in the proteasome.
source: Substrate proteins targeted for proteasomal degradation are typically conjugated with K48-linked polyubiquitin chains, which interact non-covalently with ubiquitin receptors in the proteasome (Komander and Rape, 2012; Pohl and Dikic, 2019; Swatek and Komander, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Komander and Rape, 2012; Pohl and Dikic, 2019; Swatek and Komander, 2016).

claim: UPS activity can be compromised in neurodegeneration in multiple ways, including proteasome modifications, reduced ATP level, direct inhibition by amyloid fibrils, and oxidative stress.
source: However, UPS activity can be compromised in neurodegeneration in multiple ways, including proteasome modifications, reduced ATP level, direct inhibition by amyloid fibrils, and oxidative stress (Kinger et al., 2024; McDade et al., 2024; Tseng et al., 2008; Cookson et al., 2023; Wojcik and Di Napoli, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Kinger et al., 2024; McDade et al., 2024; Tseng et al., 2008; Cookson et al., 2023; Wojcik and Di Napoli, 2004).

claim: The dynamic changes of ubiquitin have been largely overlooked in the context of neurodegeneration.
source: While these factors have been extensively studied in order to preserve proteasomal function, the dynamic changes of ubiquitin have been largely overlooked in the context of neurodegeneration.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: Ubiquitin itself undergoes post-translational modifications that can alter its structure and function.
source: Ubiquitin itself undergoes post-translational modifications that can alter its structure and function (Herhaus and Dikic, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Herhaus and Dikic, 2015).

claim: One post-translational modification of ubiquitin is phosphorylation at residue S65, installed by the kinase PINK1.
source: One such modification is phosphorylation at residue S65, installed by the kinase PINK1 (Koyano et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Koyano et al., 2014).

claim: PINK1 can exist in two forms: the full-length PINK1 localized to the mitochondrial membrane, and sPINK1, a cytosolic fragment cleaved from full-length PINK1.
source: PINK1 can exist in two forms: the full-length PINK1 localized to the mitochondrial membrane (Okatsu et al., 2015; Okatsu et al., 2013), and sPINK1, a cytosolic fragment cleaved from full-length PINK1 (Takatori et al., 2008; Yamano and Youle, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Okatsu et al., 2015; Okatsu et al., 2013; Takatori et al., 2008; Yamano and Youle, 2013).

claim: Full-length PINK1 is activated in response to mitochondrial damages, subsequently phosphorylating ubiquitin and Parkin to initiate mitophagy—a neuroprotective process for the selective removal of damaged mitochondria.
source: Full-length PINK1 is activated in response to mitochondrial damages, subsequently phosphorylating ubiquitin and Parkin to initiate mitophagy—a neuroprotective process for the selective removal of damaged mitochondria (Koyano et al., 2014; Lazarou et al., 2015; Okatsu et al., 2015; Cookson et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Koyano et al., 2014; Lazarou et al., 2015; Okatsu et al., 2015; Cookson et al., 2023).

claim: Severe and persistent mitochondrial stress can lead to mitophagy failure and sustained elevations of S65-pUb levels.
source: However, severe and persistent mitochondrial stress can also lead to mitophagy failure and sustained elevations of S65-pUb levels (Chin et al., 2023; Pollock et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Chin et al., 2023; Pollock et al., 2024).

claim: Given the prevalence of mitochondrial dysfunction under neurodegenerative conditions, pUb accumulation may result from the activation of full-length PINK1 but without effective mitophagy.
source: Given the prevalence of mitochondrial dysfunction under neurodegenerative conditions (Cookson et al., 2023), pUb accumulation may result from the activation of full-length PINK1 but without effective mitophagy.
evidence: This claim is speculative based on the understanding of mitochondrial dysfunction in neurodegeneration and cited literature (Cookson et al., 2023).

claim: The cytosolic sPINK1, processed from the full-length PINK1 by mitochondrial proteases, is normally rapidly degraded by the proteasome via the N-end rule pathway.
source: The cytosolic sPINK1, processed from the full-length PINK1 by mitochondrial proteases, is normally rapidly degraded by the proteasome via the N-end rule pathway (Takatori et al., 2008; Yamano and Youle, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Takatori et al., 2008; Yamano and Youle, 2013).

claim: As the UPS function is often compromised in neurodegeneration, sPINK1 may accumulate and phosphorylate ubiquitin, contributing to the increased pUb levels.
source: As the UPS function is often compromised in neurodegeneration (Cookson et al., 2023), sPINK1 may accumulate and phosphorylate ubiquitin, contributing to the increased pUb levels.
evidence: This claim is speculative based on the understanding of UPS dysfunction in neurodegeneration and cited literature (Cookson et al., 2023).

claim: In vitro studies have suggested that phosphorylation alters ubiquitin's structural dynamics and may affect its function.
source: In vitro studies have suggested that phosphorylation alters ubiquitin's structural dynamics and may affect its function (Dong et al., 2017; Tang and Zhang, 2020; Wauer et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Dong et al., 2017; Tang and Zhang, 2020; Wauer et al., 2015a).

claim: PINK1 phosphorylation has been shown to inhibit ubiquitin chain elongation.
source: Moreover, PINK1 phosphorylation has been shown to inhibit ubiquitin chain elongation (Wauer et al., 2015b), and the phosphomimic mutant Ub/S65E has been shown to inhibit protein turnover and reduce cell viability under stress conditions in yeast (Swaney et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Wauer et al., 2015b).

claim: The phosphomimic mutant Ub/S65E has been shown to inhibit protein turnover and reduce cell viability under stress conditions in yeast.
source: Moreover, PINK1 phosphorylation has been shown to inhibit ubiquitin chain elongation (Wauer et al., 2015b), and the phosphomimic mutant Ub/S65E has been shown to inhibit protein turnover and reduce cell viability under stress conditions in yeast (Swaney et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Swaney et al., 2015).
